title: Wildfire Smoke Shelter Placement Agent-Based Model

creators.name: Asghar, Fatima
creators.affiliation: Harrisburg University of Science and Technology, Harrisburg, PA

description:
An agent-based model of clean-air shelter access for unsheltered residents of Multnomah County, Oregon during a wildfire smoke episode.

6,842 residents — the 2025 Point-in-Time count for the county — carry individually sampled age, sex, mobility, asthma and COPD attributes drawn from published sources, start at real reported campsite locations (3,400 reports resolving to 3,317 distinct coordinates; each run seeds residents at a subset), and walk Portland's real street network (88,100 nodes after excluding freeway-only geometry) toward the nearest shelter with room. The hazard is measured hourly PM2.5 from the September 2020 smoke event, which peaked at 562.7 µg/m3 and exceeded the EPA "Unhealthy" threshold for 194 of 312 hours, in two spells — a brief crossing around hours 16–21 and the main episode beginning at hour 79.

Three primary scenarios separate the effect of total shelter capacity from the effect of how that capacity is split across sites. Scenarios B and C hold total system capacity identical at 6,842 spaces; a randomised control that draws C's ten additional sites from the same candidate pool reproduces C's sheltered count run-for-run, so the headcount difference between B and C is dispersion (more doors), with placement credit confined to shorter walks. A triage arm (scenario D) keeps B's capacity and reserves a share of beds for mobility-limited residents, closing the mobility access gap at identical aggregate access and zero added capacity. The core experiment comprises 27 runs (three scenarios × nine random seeds, 42–50), each executed from a clean working tree with a manifest recording its git commit, seed, and a SHA-256 checksum for every input file.

Built on Repast Simphony 2.11 (Java 17), with Python analysis, scenario construction and validation tooling.

Scope note: the model measures smoke exposure and inhaled particulate mass. It does not predict illness, hospitalization or death. Susceptibility weighting is deliberately held at 1.0 and equity is reported by stratification instead; see docs/final/TECHNICAL_REFERENCE.md for the citation audit that led to that decision.
